question: What are the two primary anatomical components that make up the central nervous system?

options.B: The cranial nerves and spinal nerves
options.D: The brain and the spinal cord

explanation: The central nervous system is structurally restricted to the brain and the spinal cord, whereas all nerves branching outside them belong to the peripheral nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why does white matter appear white in freshly dissected central nervous system tissue?

options.A: Accumulated cerebrospinal fluid within the interstitial spaces
options.B: A high concentration of unmyelinated neuronal cell bodies
options.C: The presence of dense connective tissue coverings
options.D: The abundance of lipid-rich myelin sheaths wrapping axon tracts

explanation: Myelin is a fatty substance that insulates axons and imparts a whitish sheen to nerve tracts, distinguishing them from grey matter cell bodies. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which meningeal layer lies directly against the surface of the cerebral cortex, following all its contours?
explanation: The pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer that intimately adheres to every fold and fissure of the brain surface. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary function of cerebrospinal fluid circulating within the meningeal spaces?

options.A: Acting as a hydraulic shock absorber to protect neural tissue
options.B: Synthesizing neurotransmitters for the cerebral cortex
options.C: Supplying primary oxygen demands to deep brain nuclei
options.D: Secreting hormones directly into the systemic bloodstream

explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid buoys the brain within the skull, dramatically reducing its effective weight and buffering mechanical shocks. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h2)

question: Which lobe of the cerebral cortex contains the primary visual processing center?
explanation: The occipital lobe located at the posterior pole of the brain is dedicated primarily to processing visual information. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h3)

question: A patient stroke survivor can produce fluent sentences, but the words make no sense and they fail to comprehend spoken questions. Which cortical region is most likely damaged?
explanation: Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe governs language comprehension; damage here causes fluent but nonsensical speech output. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h3)

question: Which diencephalic structure functions as the primary relay station for sensory input heading to the cerebral cortex?
explanation: Almost all sensory pathways synapse in the thalamus before being projected to the appropriate primary sensory cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h4)

question: What makes an injury to the medulla oblongata immediately life-threatening?

options.A: It controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement across the body
options.B: It houses vital autonomic centers controlling respiration and heart rate
options.C: It contains the primary visual and auditory processing areas
options.D: It produces all the cerebrospinal fluid circulating in the ventricles

explanation: The medulla oblongata contains the cardiac, vasomotor, and respiratory rhythm centers essential for basic life support. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary function of the cerebellum in the central nervous system?

options.A: Processing conscious thought and complex reasoning
options.B: Producing hormones that regulate systemic metabolism
options.C: Relaying visual and auditory impulses to the cerebrum
options.D: Coordinating smooth voluntary movement and balance

explanation: The cerebellum fine-tunes motor activity and maintains equilibrium based on real-time sensory feedback. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h5)

question: A patient presents with an unsteady, staggering gait and an inability to smoothly touch their own nose with their finger. Which brain structure is most likely impaired?
explanation: Symptoms like ataxia and dysmetria are classic indicators of cerebellar dysfunction affecting motor coordination. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h5)

question: Through which spinal nerve root do sensory signals enter the spinal cord?
explanation: Afferent sensory fibers enter the spinal cord via the dorsal root, carrying impulses from peripheral receptors. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the physiological advantage of spinal reflex arcs?

options.A: They enable conscious control over internal visceral organs
options.B: They allow rapid responses to danger without waiting for brain processing
options.C: They prevent sensory signals from ever reaching the brain
options.D: They increase the speed of thought processing in the cerebral cortex

explanation: Reflexes integrate at the spinal cord level to produce immediate, protective reactions before conscious perception occurs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h6)

question: Where is cerebrospinal fluid primarily produced within the brain?
explanation: Caporous networks of choroid plexuses inside the ventricular system filter blood plasma to produce cerebrospinal fluid. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h7)

question: Which structural feature is primarily responsible for forming the tight permeability restrictions of the blood-brain barrier?

options.A: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells
options.B: Large fenestrations within the cerebral arterioles
options.C: A thick layer of external periosteal bone
options.D: The absence of any glial support cells around neurons

explanation: Endothelial cells in brain capillaries are fused by tight junctions, preventing unconstrained paracellular movement of substances from blood to brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h7)
